title: The simplex algorithm: what is the table doing?

els.text: Explain what each step of the simplex table is doing, and why it works.

•  Say what the starting table means
•  Choose where to go next, and how far
•  Know when to stop
A plan is a corner of the region

els.latex: \begin{array}{l}\text{Maximise } P = 2x + 3y\\[2ex]\text{subject to}\\[1.4ex] 2x + y \le 10\\[1ex] x + 2y \le 8\\[1ex] x \ge 0,\; y \ge 0\end{array}

els.text: Each corner is a possible plan.

slides.brief: The one worked problem for the whole deck. The corners come on the first click and their values of P on the second.
slides.title: The problem

els.text: 2.  Move along an edge to a corner where $P$ is bigger.
3.  Stop when no edge goes uphill.
We do not check every corner. The table tells us which way to walk.
They turn each limit into an equation

$s_1$ is the amount of the first limit not used.
$s_2$ is the amount of the second not used.
At the start $x = 0$ and $y = 0$, so $s_1 = 10$, $s_2 = 8$ and $P = 0$.
Each row is one of the equations

Read it: the variables in the first column are the ones that are not zero.
$s_1 = 10$, $s_2 = 8$, $P = 0$, and $x = y = 0$.
The bottom row says how fast $P$ grows
$-2$ under $x$: raise $x$ by 1 and $P$ goes up by 2.
$-3$ under $y$: raise $y$ by 1 and $P$ goes up by 3.
The most negative entry is the way to go: $y$.

slides.title: Which way? Look at the bottom row

els.text: Raise $y$ until a limit runs out
The smallest ratio is 4: the second limit runs out first. $y$ goes up to 4.

slides.brief: Only the positive entries in the chosen column are used for the ratios.
slides.title: How far? The ratios

els.text: Rewrite every equation from the new corner

els.latex: \begin{array}{l}\mathrm{NPR} = \mathrm{R}3 \div 2 \quad \text{(divide the pivot row)}\\[1ex] \mathrm{R}1 + 3 \times \mathrm{NPR} \quad \text{(take } y \text{ out of the bottom row)}\\[1ex] \mathrm{R}2 - \mathrm{NPR} \quad \text{(take } y \text{ out of the first limit)}\end{array}

els.text: Now $y$ is in the first column: $y = 4$, and $P = 12$.

slides.brief: The row operations first, then the new table on the first click.
slides.title: Moving there: row operations

els.text: $s_2 = 0$: the second limit is used up. That is why we stopped.
The new bottom row is the news
$-\tfrac{1}{2}$ under $x$: raising $x$ still helps. By how much?
But $y$ must fall by $\tfrac{1}{2}$: $P$ falls by $3 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 1\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Net: $2 - 1\tfrac{1}{2} = +\tfrac{1}{2}$. The bottom row already did this sum.

slides.brief: The key idea: each entry in the bottom row is the net effect, after everything else adjusts.
slides.title: The trade-off

els.text: Raise $x$ until a limit runs out
The smallest is 4: the first limit runs out first. $x$ goes up to 4, and $y$ comes down to 2.

els.latex: \begin{array}{l}\mathrm{NPR} = \mathrm{R}2 \div \tfrac{3}{2} \quad \text{(divide the pivot row)}\\[1ex] \mathrm{R}1 + \tfrac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{NPR} \quad \text{(take } x \text{ out of the bottom row)}\\[1ex] \mathrm{R}3 - \tfrac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{NPR} \quad \text{(take } x \text{ out of the } y \text{ row)}\end{array}

els.text: When the bottom row has no negatives
$s_1$ and $s_2$ cannot be negative, so any move can only lower $P$.
Maximum: $P = 14$ at $x = 4$, $y = 2$. Both limits are used up.

els.latex: \begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\text{step}&\text{in / out}&\text{corner}&P\\\hline \text{start}&&(0,0)&0\\ 1&y \text{ in, } s_2 \text{ out}&(0,4)&12\\ 2&x \text{ in, } s_1 \text{ out}&(4,2)&14\end{array}

els.text: Each step moved to a better corner. We never visited $(5, 0)$, where $P = 10$.
$y$ came in first, then went back down as $x$ came in: the walk is not always straight up.

•  Pivot column: the most negative entry in the bottom row.
•  Pivot row: the smallest ratio, right-hand side divided by the positive entries in that column.
•  Divide the pivot row by the pivot. Take away multiples of it from every other row.
•  Stop when the bottom row has no negatives. Read the variables from the first column.

•  Ratios: only for positive entries in the pivot column.
•  Update the bottom row too: it is a row like the others.
•  A variable not in the first column is 0, even if you were using it a step ago.
•  Stopping early: check the whole bottom row, not just the first entry.

summary: One worked problem from start to finish: slack variables, the starting table, which way to go (the bottom row), how far (the ratios), the row operations that move to the next corner, the trade-off in the new bottom row, and when to stop. A graph beside the table shows the walk from corner to corner.
